solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Show pages out of order

indicators.note: read as 'outside', so the first item sits round the second rather than coming from it

blocks.note: PP is the standard abbreviation for pages
the Order of Merit, a British honour, abbreviated OM

explanation.surface: A display or exhibition whose pages have been bound in the wrong sequence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of order' looks like a single phrase meaning jumbled, but it splits: 'out of' is the wrapper and 'order' is the Order of Merit.
explanation.definitionFit: Pomp is ceremonial splendour, a grand public display or spectacle.

clue.text: Twisted rake's broken with holes

indicators.note: something broken is split open, so the outer word parts to let the rake in

blocks.note: pitted means marked with small holes
a roué is a debauched man, a rake

explanation.surface: A garden rake has snapped and its tines are full of holes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rake' is not the garden tool but the old word for a debauched man about town.
explanation.definitionFit: A dancer who pirouetted spun round on one foot, i.e. twisted or turned.

clue.text: I am less "parleyed", perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps says this is only one possible form, so the letters may come in another order

blocks.note: all fifteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone declares they will be holding fewer talks.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the fodder and the meaning: someone who has been 'parleyed' less has had less said, which is what this phrase promises.
explanation.definitionFit: The stock phrase is a promise to keep a secret, refusing to talk about something.

clue.text: See increase in value

blocks.note: first meaning: understand or recognise, as in 'I see your point'
second meaning: what assets such as houses do over time

explanation.surface: A financial tip: watch your investment grow.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers both grasping something fully and rising in worth, as property prices do.

clue.text: Man still talking

indicators.note: talking means the word is heard spoken, so its sound counts rather than its spelling

blocks.note: still, as in calm and quiet, is peace

explanation.surface: A man who keeps on talking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'still' looks like an adverb meaning yet; it is the adjective for calm.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess or draughts each playing piece is called a man.

clue.text: Checks unlikely to be put in again

blocks.note: to rein in is to check or restrain
a tall story is an unlikely one

explanation.surface: Bank cheques are unlikely to be deposited a second time.
explanation.walkthrough: TALL means unlikely only in the phrase 'tall story' or 'tall tale'.
explanation.definitionFit: To reinstall software or a fitting is to put it in place once more.

clue.text: Song about potty arrangement of lifts?

indicators.note: about means around, so the song is placed on either side of the next word

blocks.note: a carol is a festive song
a po is a chamber pot, a potty

explanation.surface: A song about a crazy scheme for elevators.
explanation.walkthrough: 'potty' reads as crazy; it is the chamber pot. 'Lifts' are car rides, not elevators.
explanation.definitionFit: A car pool is a scheme where commuters share rides, giving each other lifts in turn.

clue.text: Ready for a shower?

blocks.note: surface reading: prepared to step under the water
setter's reading: ready is slang for cash, and a shower is someone who shows up at an event

explanation.walkthrough: 'shower' is one who shows, not a wash, and 'ready' is the noun for cash (readies).
explanation.definitionFit: Appearance money is a fee paid to a celebrity or athlete simply for turning up at an event.

clue.text: Choke as you're eating a piece of cake

indicators.note: the words before it are eating, holding the answer inside them across the word gaps

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A warning that you might choke while eating cake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a piece of cake' looks like what is being eaten, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece of cake is an idiom for something simple to do.

clue.text: Badger forbidden for stew

blocks.note: to rag is to tease or pester
out means not allowed, as in 'that's out'

explanation.surface: Badger meat is banned from use in a stew.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badger' is the verb meaning pester, not the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A ragout is a richly seasoned meat and vegetable stew.

clue.text: Free rent again

blocks.note: first meaning: let go, set loose
second meaning: let out a property once more

explanation.surface: A tenant's plea for the property to be rent-free once the lease is renewed.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense splits the word as re-lease, to lease a second time.
explanation.definitionFit: To release a prisoner is to set them at liberty; to re-lease a flat is to let it out once more.

clue.text: Breaks in its covers vibrate the wrong way

indicators.note: going the wrong way means running backwards, so the word for vibrate is read in reverse
something that covers another goes round it, so the first word wraps the second

blocks.note: taken as written, then split to go round the next piece
a cat's purr is a vibrating hum

explanation.surface: Something breaks into a machine and makes its casing shake in the wrong direction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'its' is used literally: its first letter stays in front and its last two follow the reversed word.
explanation.definitionFit: To irrupt is to burst or force one's way in suddenly, as a crowd breaks into a building.

clue.text: Cowboy on plains sure of getting shot

definitions.note: used attributively, as in 'cowboy builders', to match the adjective

indicators.note: something shot to pieces is wrecked, so the letters before it are blown apart and rebuilt

blocks.note: the fourteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A Western gunfighter on the prairie, certain he will be shot.
explanation.walkthrough: The Wild West picture hides the British sense of cowboy: a shoddy, unqualified tradesman.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a cowboy is a careless, incompetent worker, so cowboy work is amateurish and slipshod.

clue.text: Teams in Italy agreed on title

blocks.note: a posse is a band or team of people
si is Italian for yes
taken as written

explanation.surface: Serie A clubs reach a deal over a league championship.
explanation.definitionFit: In law, title means ownership or the right to possess something.

clue.text: Look, tramp returned sandwiches to restaurant

indicators.note: something returned comes back the way it went, so the words before it are read backwards
a sandwich has filling between its slices, so the reversed letters go round the next word

blocks.note: an air is a look or manner, as in 'an air of authority'
a disparaging word for a promiscuous woman
taken as written

explanation.surface: A vagrant turns back and takes sandwiches to an eatery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look' and 'tramp' are reversed together as one unit before the split; 'to' looks like a link word but is the filling.
explanation.definitionFit: A trattoria is an informal Italian eating house, a kind of restaurant.

clue.text: Give denial about dessert I had

blocks.note: re means concerning
pud is short for pudding, British for dessert
I ate, read as had in the sense of consumed

explanation.surface: Someone denies having eaten the pudding.
explanation.definitionFit: To repudiate a claim is to reject or deny it outright.

clue.text: Plain backing on everything

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the whole phrase after it is read in reverse

blocks.note: taken as written
all means everything

explanation.surface: A plain-coloured fabric used as a backing for everything.
explanation.definitionFit: A llano is a grassy treeless plain of the kind found in northern South America.

clue.text: In spite of that, almost square

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter of the phrase is dropped

blocks.note: even so means nevertheless

explanation.surface: Something is nearly square despite everything.
explanation.definitionFit: Two sides that are evens or square are level, all debts settled.

clue.text: Troublemaker, terrorist? Not to criminal

indicators.note: not means leave out, so those two letters are taken away
criminal suggests something crooked, so what remains is twisted into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A troublemaker is a terrorist? No, just a criminal.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing one T and the O from TERRORIST leaves ERRRIST to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A stirrer is someone who deliberately stirs up trouble or ill-feeling.

clue.text: Spain and France open royal houses for white people

indicators.note: the houses are opened up so that something can be put inside them

blocks.note: royals live in palaces
E is the international vehicle code for Spain
F is the vehicle code for France

explanation.surface: Two European monarchies throw their palaces open to visitors from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: International vehicle registration codes are a common source of single letters for countries.
explanation.definitionFit: Paleface was the name supposedly given to white people by Native Americans in Western fiction.

clue.text: Try to get information about alien thing?

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the first word goes round the second

blocks.note: to fish is to angle for facts
E.T., the film's extraterrestrial

explanation.surface: Probing for facts about an extraterrestrial object.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thing' is used as in 'to have a thing about' something.
explanation.definitionFit: A fetish is an obsession, the kind of fixation one calls having a thing about something.

clue.text: Old hat with paper covering

blocks.note: first meaning: out of date, old-fashioned
second meaning, read literally: positioned at the back of a well-known newspaper that hides you

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense pictures someone hidden behind a copy of The Times, the London daily newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: Being behind the times means out of step with current fashion, just as old hat things are stale.

clue.text: Husband slightly bent

blocks.note: abbreviation for husband
a bit means slightly

explanation.surface: A husband who is a little stooped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bent' looks like crooked or stooped; it is the noun for an inclination.
explanation.definitionFit: A bent is a natural tendency, just as a habit is a settled tendency of behaviour.

clue.text: Hairy man in union full of it

indicators.note: something full of another has it inside, so the union holds the next item

blocks.note: the European Union
it means sex appeal, abbreviated SA

explanation.surface: A shaggy fellow in a trade union who's full of himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it' as sex appeal is an old convention, from Clara Bow, the 'It girl'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis Esau, Jacob's twin, is described as a hairy man.

clue.text: Very short rope for tanning rooms

indicators.note: short means cut off before the end, so the last letter of the rope goes

blocks.note: so means very, as in 'so good'
a lariat is a lasso, a rope with a noose

explanation.surface: A very short rope set aside for a tanning salon, perhaps to hang towels.
explanation.definitionFit: A solarium is a room for sunbathing or using sunbeds; solaria is its Latin plural.

clue.text: Dog found one crossing US state

blocks.note: to found something is to base or establish it
NJ is the postal abbreviation for New Jersey
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A dog is discovered crossing a state line in America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crossing' places the I on the far side of the state: BASE, then NJ, then I.
explanation.definitionFit: The basenji is a barkless African hunting dog breed.

clue.text: Regularly turned pants near the bottom

indicators.note: regularly means at fixed intervals, so every other letter of the following word is kept
pants is slang for rubbish, so the words after it are in a poor, muddled state

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters
the seven letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Underwear turned inside out at intervals, close to someone's backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pants' looks like the noun for underwear; it is the British slang for rubbish, signalling a jumble. 'the' belongs to the fodder, not the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun the underneath is the underside or lowest part of something, its bottom.

clue.text: Scottish Herald — the end of all that

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that is taken

blocks.note: the final letter of the word
yon is an old or dialect word for that, as in 'yon hill'

explanation.surface: A Scottish newspaper declares the end of everything.
explanation.walkthrough: The Herald is a Glasgow newspaper, but here a herald is a heraldic officer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lord Lyon King of Arms is Scotland's chief heraldic officer, usually called simply the Lyon.
